ABOUT THIS EDITION

Open God's Word in Contemporary Chichewa (Mawu a Mulungu mu Chichewa Chalero), also distributed as the CCL, is a full Bible in the Chichewa language, published by Biblica with an initial New Testament copyright of 2002 and a complete Bible edition in 2016. It is made available under an open MIT License. The full Bible was launched in Malawi in late 2017, making it the first contemporary-language full Bible in Chichewa. The project reportedly took three generations of effort to complete. While Chichewa has had Scripture since the early 1900s -- the traditional Buku Lopatulika (Holy Bible) was first printed in 1922, translated by a commission of Dutch Reformed Church missionaries and Malawian contributors -- that version uses archaic language that many younger readers find difficult to understand. The Chewa people are the largest ethnic group in Malawi, and Chichewa/Nyanja, a Bantu language, is the de facto language of national identity in Malawi; this contemporary translation was designed to be accessible to modern Chichewa speakers across Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique.

1. The Beginning

Genesis 1:1

The story of Jesus fits within the larger story of the Judeo Christian tradition. The purpose of everything since creation has been to point to the life of Jesus. All of creation speaks of the majesty of God. As God created man and woman he intended them to live in peace with him forever. But because of their disobedience mankind was separated from God. But God still loved mankind so throughout the Scriptures God reveals his plan to save the world.

2. Birth Of Jesus

Luke 1:1

Luke makes his introduction as the careful author of this Gospel. The angel Gabriel appears to Mary, a virgin in Nazareth. He announces to her that she has found favor with God and will give birth to Jesus, the Son of God. Through Jesus' birth, prophecies are fulfilled by the arrangement of events. God leaves no detail unnoticed. The same can be said of our own lives.

3. Childhood Of Jesus

Luke 2:21

One week after the baby is born, He is circumcised and officially named Jesus. While Jesus is a small boy they go to the temple where they meet a man named Simeon. The Holy Spirit had assured Simeon he would not die before seeing the Lord's Messiah. Simeon sees Jesus and declares Him the promised Messiah.

4. Baptism Of Jesus By John

Luke 3:1

John the Baptist calls out in the desert. He preaches by the river Jordan, "Turn away from your sins and be baptized, and God will forgive your sins." He is the one Isaiah predicted would make way for the Lord. The crowds gather. Immediately, he warns them not to only say they have repented. Instead, they're to follow repentance with actions that exhibit a changed heart. Jesus is baptized and receives the Holy Spirit. He kneels at the feet of someone lesser than Himself to be baptized. He demonstrates how we are to be humble.

5. The Devil Tempts Jesus

Luke 4:1

After Jesus has been baptized, He's led by the Spirit into the desert. He spends 40 days there, constantly tempted by the devil. All that time, he eats nothing. The devil tries to tempt Jesus, but Jesus answers using Scripture, resisting him.

6. Jesus Proclaims Fulfillment Of The Scriptures

Luke 4:14

When Jesus returns to Nazareth, He goes to the synagogue. He's asked to read the Scriptures and is handed the Book of Isaiah. From it, He reads Isaiah 61:1-2. The prophecy speaks of bringing good news to the poor, proclaiming liberty to the captives, recovery of sight to the blind, freeing the oppressed, and announcing that it's time the Lord will save His people. When He finishes reading, Jesus announces to the people that the prophecy has come true as it was just read.

7. Parable Of The Pharisee And Tax Collector

Luke 18:9

Jesus teaches from a boat off the shore of Lake Gennesaret. He speaks in parables, giving the example of a Pharisee and tax collector going to the temple to pray. The two men approach prayer very differently. The Pharisee in the story stands by himself and lists his respectable attributes. He thanks God that he is not greedy, dishonest, or an adulterer like everyone else. He specifically points out the tax collector and thanks God for not being like him. The Pharisee boldly tells God what he does: He fasts two days a week and gives a tenth of his income. The tax collector stands at a distance from the altar. Head bowed, he beats on his chest. The only thing he prays is, "God, have pity on me, a sinner!"

8. Miraculous Catch Of Fish

Luke 5:1

Jesus tells the fisherman who owns it to push out farther and let down their nets. The fisherman grumbles that he and the others have already been out all night long. They didn't catch anything. The fisherman agrees to go out and calls to his partners. Jesus sits in the boat with the fisherman. He waits expectantly. Then gathers the nets, slowly bringing something to the surface. He laughs with joy when he sees the nets are full of flopping fish. When they're done, the fisherman sits in a boat full of fish. He looks up to Jesus. The fisherman frowns and says, "Go away from me, Lord. I am a sinful man." Jesus tells him not to be afraid, that from then on, he would be a fisher of men.

Luke 8:41

Crowds press in on Jesus as He leaves the synagogue. One voice rises above the others. A man, Jairus, begs Jesus to save his sick, 12-year-old daughter. Another man runs up to Jairus. He tells him not to bother the teacher, that his daughter has died. Jesus turns and tells him not to be afraid. And that if Jairus would believe, his daughter would be well. Jesus and the disciples visit the family. The neighbors wail for the loss of the daughter. She lies lifeless on a cot. Jesus looks at her for a moment. Then He looks to the child’s mother and comforts her. He says the child isn't dead, but that she’s actually just asleep. Jesus sits and looks at the girl for a moment, then tells her to rise.

The Gospel opens with the eternal Word who was with God and was God, made flesh in Jesus. John the Baptist bears witness to him, and the first disciples follow the one Andrew calls the Messiah.

You Must Be Born Again

Nicodemus comes to Jesus by night and hears that no one can see the kingdom of God without being born again. God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son.

The Woman at the Well

Jesus offers living water to a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well, and many Samaritans believe in him. Returning to Galilee, he heals a royal official's dying son with a word.

Healing at the Pool of Bethesda

John 5

John 5

Healing at the Pool of Bethesda

On the Sabbath Jesus heals a man who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years. When the leaders object, Jesus declares that the Son gives life and does the works of his Father.

The Bread of Life

John 6

John 6

The Bread of Life

Jesus feeds five thousand with five loaves and two fish, then walks across the sea to his disciples. Declaring himself the bread of life, he watches many turn away while Peter confesses that he alone has the words of eternal life.

Jesus goes up to Jerusalem in secret, then teaches openly in the temple courts. On the last day of the festival he invites the thirsty to come to him and drink, and the crowd is divided over who he is.

The Man Born Blind

The Raising of Lazarus

Jesus weeps at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, then calls him out of the grave after four days. The sign leads many to believe, and the council resolves that Jesus must die.

Jesus comforts his disciples: he goes to prepare a place in his Father's house, and he himself is the way to the Father. He promises the Holy Spirit and leaves them his peace.

Jesus is the true vine and his disciples are the branches, called to remain in him and bear fruit. He commands them to love one another and warns that the world will hate them as it hated him.

Jesus promises the Spirit of truth, who will convict the world and guide the disciples into all truth. Their grief will turn to joy: 'Take heart! I have overcome the world.'

Jesus lifts his eyes to heaven and prays for himself, for his disciples, and for all who will believe through their message. He asks that they may be one, as he and the Father are one.

he 1906 Chichewa (Nyanja) New Testament, titled Chipangano Chatsopano, was issued by the National Bible Society of Scotland from translations prepared by the two Scottish Presbyterian missions on opposite shores of Lake Nyasa. At Blantyre in the south the Church of Scotland mission worked under David Clement Scott, whose Cyclopaedic Dictionary of the Mang'anja Language (1892) established much of the lexical base. At Livingstonia in the north the Free Church mission worked under Robert Laws, whose team had produced earlier Gospel portions from the 1880s.

Bringing the two mission committees into a single text required arbitration over dialect, orthography, and key theological terms, particularly the rendering of God's name and the verbs for redemption and atonement. The National Bible Society of Scotland, which had funded Scripture work in Nyasaland since the Livingstone era, sponsored the unified edition.

The 1906 New Testament circulated from the two mission stations and the network of village schools attached to them, where Chichewa had become the vehicle of Presbyterian primary education. Literacy in Chichewa, fostered by catechism and Scripture reading, grew alongside the text. The Blantyre and Livingstonia missions would merge their ecclesiastical structures in 1926 as the Church of Central Africa Presbyterian, and the 1906 New Testament served both streams until the revision that produced the complete Chichewa Bible of 1922.

Chichewa (also called Nyanja) is the national language of Malawi and is spoken by about twelve million people across Malawi, Zambia, and Mozambique.

The Chichewa biblical tradition traces to the Scottish Presbyterian mission at Blantyre, founded in 1876 after David Livingstone's death. A parallel Chichewa (Union Shire) Bible came out of the Dutch Reformed mission at Mvera, and the two traditions were merged in the Union Nyanja Bible of 1936, which remained the standard text through the 1960s.

The 1966 Genesis portion draws on the 1936 Union text. It was intended for school and adult literacy programs in the new republic, where Chichewa had been declared a national language in 1968. estamente Watsopano wa Mwini Watu Ndi Mpulumutsi Yesu Kristu, the 1900 Chinyanja (Chewa) New Testament, was produced by the British and Foreign Bible Society for the Presbyterian missions on the shores of Lake Nyasa. The translation drew on decades of work by the Livingstonia Mission (Free Church of Scotland) at Bandawe and Khondowe and the Blantyre Mission (Church of Scotland) in the Shire Highlands, following the routes opened by David Livingstone's Zambesi expedition of 1858-1864.

Chinyanja, also called Chewa or Nyanja, is a Bantu language of the Niger-Congo family spoken across the Shire valley, the Lake Malawi basin, and into eastern Zambia and Mozambique. The 1900 New Testament followed Luke (1877), Acts (1883), and a combined Matthew-Mark-John volume, consolidating a working text for catechumens, schools, and congregational reading. The Scottish mission translators standardized Chinyanja spelling along the lines of the UMCA's Chinyanja at Likoma Island, producing a shared written register used across Presbyterian, Anglican, and Dutch Reformed missions.

The book became a staple of the African evangelist corps trained at the Overtoun Institution at Khondowe, whose graduates carried it across Nyasaland and into Northern Rhodesia during the opening decade of British Central African colonial administration under Sir Harry Johnston and Sir Alfred Sharpe.

It is a paperback Bible Society portion in standard format, used in the Church of Central Africa Presbyterian, the Anglican Diocese of Southern Malawi, the Dutch Reformed (later CCAP Nkhoma) congregations, and parallel Chichewa work in Zambia and Mozambique.

uku Lopatulika ndilo Mau a Mulungu Chipangano cha Kale ndi cha Tsopano, the Holy Book which is the Word of God, Old Covenant and New, is the 1922 Chinyanja Bible issued by the British and Foreign Bible Society for the Chewa-speaking Christian communities of Nyasaland (now Malawi) and adjoining regions. The title page presents the work as a full Bible in the Chewa dialect of Nyanja, the Bantu language of the Lake Malawi basin.

Nyanja Bible translation began in the 1880s with portions prepared at the Church of Scotland Mission at Blantyre (founded 1876) and at the Livingstonia Mission of the Free Church of Scotland at Cape Maclear and later Bandawe and Livingstonia (founded 1875). Missionary linguists including William Koyi, Robert Laws, David Clement Scott, and Alexander Hetherwick produced a succession of gospel, portion, and Testament editions through the 1890s and 1900s. The complete Bible committee drew on these earlier labors and on the catechetical vocabulary of the two Scottish missions.

The 1922 printing is listed by Darlow and Moule among the Nyanja entries in Volume 2, Part 3, of the Historical Catalogue. The edition was distributed from the BFBS depot at Blantyre to Presbyterian, Anglican (Universities' Mission to Central Africa), and Dutch Reformed Church stations across the Nyasa and Shire districts. The Chewa text of this Bible became the liturgical standard for Chichewa-speaking Protestant churches in Malawi, eastern Zambia, and Mozambique through the twentieth century.
